$comment: Stylised, systems-level region metadata for dimagh. Positions are in a normalised brain-space (x = left(-)/right(+), y = inferior(-)/superior(+), z = posterior(-)/anterior(+)) and are anatomically INSPIRED, not anatomically measured. Copy is written for someone with no background in neuroscience: plain words everywhere except the names of brain parts, which are the one thing worth learning. Precision is kept by saying 'one of the parts involved in' rather than 'the X centre' — no region here does one job on its own.

regions.name: Retina
regions.summary: The back of your eye, where light turns into a signal.
regions.role: A thin sheet of nerve tissue lining the back of each eye. Light hits it, and cells there turn it into electrical signals. Other cells in the same sheet already start picking out edges and colour before anything is sent to the brain.
regions.why: Your eye is not a camera sending raw pictures inward. It edits first, and throws a lot away. Everything that happens later is working on that edited version — never on the original.
regions.caveat: We draw it as one glowing patch. It is really a layered circuit with dozens of cell types and well over a hundred million light-sensitive cells.

regions.name: Optic Pathway
regions.summary: The cable from your eyes — and the junction where it crosses over.
regions.role: The nerve bundles leaving both eyes. They meet, and part of each one crosses to the other side. After the crossing, signals are grouped by which part of the world you are looking at, rather than by which eye saw it.
regions.why: That regrouping is why damage in slightly different places causes very different kinds of blindness. The wiring layout is doing a job, not just carrying traffic.
regions.caveat: Shown as one short tube. It is really several named sections with their own rules about what crosses over and what does not.

regions.name: Thalamic Visual Relay
regions.summary: A gate between your eyes and the rest of your brain.
regions.role: A waystation deep in the middle of the brain that visual signals pass through on their way to the surface. It is not a plain wire: how awake you are, and what the rest of the brain is already doing, both change how much gets through.
regions.why: Most of the connections arriving here come back *down* from the brain, not up from the eye. Even this early, what you let through depends on what you were already expecting.
regions.caveat: Treated as a single gate. It is really layered, with separate lanes carrying different kinds of visual information.

regions.name: Primary Visual Cortex
regions.summary: The first place in the brain that gets a map of what you are looking at.
regions.role: Sits at the very back of your head. It holds a map of your field of view, and different cells in it react to different small details: the angle of an edge, how sharp it is, which way it is moving.
regions.why: There is no picture here. Your visual world is being held as a huge pile of small measurements, and everything you consciously see gets built back up out of them.
regions.caveat: We show the different details as separate layers so you can see them. In a real brain they are all tangled together in the same tissue.

regions.name: Early Visual Association Areas
regions.summary: Where small details start becoming shapes, surfaces and colours.
regions.role: The next step after the first visual map. Here the small details get joined up: lines continue across gaps, surfaces get a colour, textures appear. It also starts correcting colour for the lighting in the room.
regions.why: This is why an apple looks red under a warm lamp and under cold daylight, even though the light bouncing off it is genuinely a different colour in each case. Your brain is guessing the apple, not reporting the light.
regions.caveat: Two separate areas are drawn as one node here. They behave differently from each other.

regions.name: Motion-Sensitive Visual Area
regions.summary: Specialised for movement — which way, and how fast.
regions.role: Packed with cells that each care about one direction and speed of movement. Together they work out whether something is moving across your view, and where it is going.
regions.why: Stare at a waterfall, look away, and the rocks seem to drift upward. That happens because the cells tuned to downward motion get tired, and the ones tuned to upward motion win by default.
regions.caveat: Motion is handled by several areas working together. This is one well-studied piece of that, not the whole thing.

regions.name: Object-Selective Cortex
regions.summary: Where a pile of details finally becomes 'a thing'.
regions.role: Responds much more to a whole, sensible object than to the same shapes jumbled up. Its response stays roughly the same if the object moves, turns, or gets bigger or smaller.
regions.why: That stability is the whole trick of recognition. It is why you know it is the same apple from across the room, at an angle, in worse light.
regions.caveat: The 'apple' is spread across a pattern of activity in many cells. There is no single cell, and no single spot, that is the apple.

regions.name: Ventral Temporal Cortex
regions.summary: Sorts what you see into broad kinds: faces, places, words, objects.
regions.role: A stretch along the underside of the brain where the pattern of activity is reliably different for faces, for places, for written words, for bodies, and for things you can pick up.
regions.why: It shows that your visual system is not organised by shape or colour. It is organised by what things *are* — which is a much stranger and more useful thing for it to be doing.
regions.caveat: These areas overlap and blur into each other. They are not separate boxes with clean edges.

regions.name: Primary Auditory Cortex
regions.summary: The first place sound arrives, laid out like a piano keyboard.
regions.role: Arranged by pitch: nearby patches of tissue respond to nearby notes. It is also quick to pick up when a sound starts and how it changes over time.
regions.why: Speech, music and a slammed door all reach your ear as nothing but changing air pressure. The first job is turning that into something with pitch and timing you can work with.
regions.caveat: Drawn as one patch. There are really several areas here, each tuned a little differently.

regions.name: Auditory Association Cortex
regions.summary: Where sound starts turning into speech.
regions.role: Reacts to complicated, structured sounds, and gets especially busy during speech. It tracks the rhythm of syllables and phrases as they go past.
regions.why: Hearing a word is not the same as hearing a noise. Somewhere around here a continuous stream of sound gets chopped into pieces that can be matched against words you know.
regions.caveat: Both sides of the brain do this, though not equally. Splitting it neatly into 'sound' and then 'speech sounds' is a convenient simplification.

regions.name: Posterior Temporal Language Region
regions.summary: Connects a word to what it means.
regions.role: Usually on the left side. It helps link the sound or spelling of a word to everything you know about the thing it refers to.
regions.why: Damage around here can leave someone speaking fluently and confidently while the words no longer mean much. That split tells us form and meaning are handled separately.
regions.caveat: Language is a network, not a spot. The old idea of a single 'language area' here is now considered far too simple.

regions.name: Inferior Frontal Language Region
regions.summary: Puts words in order, and picks between ones that compete.
regions.role: Near the left temple. Busy when a sentence needs structure, when several possible words are fighting to come out, and when sounds need sequencing to be spoken.
regions.why: Speaking is not looking words up in a list. Several candidates come up at once and something has to settle it — fast, every few hundred milliseconds, all day.
regions.caveat: Often called 'Broca's area'. It does several different jobs, and plenty of them have nothing to do with language.

regions.name: Somatosensory Cortex
regions.summary: A map of your body, for touch and for where your limbs are.
regions.role: A strip running over the top of your head holding a map of your skin — but a lopsided one. Lips, face and hands take up far more space than your back or your legs.
regions.why: When you move, this is how you find out what happened. Without it you can still move, but you become clumsy and cannot correct yourself.
regions.caveat: The map is not fixed. It shifts with practice, with injury, and across a lifetime.

regions.name: Primary Motor Cortex
regions.summary: The main exit. Where a plan becomes an actual movement.
regions.role: Sends signals down the spinal cord that drive your muscles. What it cares about is more like direction and force than individual muscles.
regions.why: This is the narrow doorway everything has to pass through to become a real event in the world. Everything before it is just intention.
regions.caveat: It does not store the movement. It is one stage in a loop that also runs through the cerebellum, the basal ganglia, your spinal cord and your senses.

regions.name: Premotor & Planning Cortex
regions.summary: Works out the movement before you make it.
regions.role: Sits just in front of the motor exit. It becomes active *before* you move, while the movement is being chosen, ordered and prepared — including movements you prepare and then hold back.
regions.why: You can measure preparation starting before people say they decided to move. That gap is one of the most argued-over findings in the whole field.
regions.caveat: What that early activity means for free will is genuinely unsettled. We show the timing; we do not take a side.

regions.name: Frontal Eye Fields
regions.summary: Decides where to look next — and where to pay attention.
regions.role: Helps aim your eyes. It also helps aim your attention at a spot without moving your eyes there at all.
regions.why: Looking and attending share machinery. Paying attention to something out of the corner of your eye uses much of what would have moved your eyes to it.
regions.caveat: Attention does not have one controller. This is one part of a network spread across the front and top of the brain.

regions.name: Posterior Parietal Cortex
regions.summary: Keeps track of where things are and which ones matter.
regions.role: Pulls together what you can see, where your body is, and what you are trying to do, into a sense of the space around you — including a running ranking of what in it is worth your attention.
regions.why: Damage here can leave someone behaving as though the left half of the world simply stopped being relevant. They can see it. It just stops mattering to them.
regions.caveat: The 'ranking' is a way of describing what the activity does. It is not a structure you could find under a microscope.

regions.name: Temporoparietal Junction
regions.summary: Interrupts you when something unexpected happens.
regions.role: Part of a more automatic kind of attention. It reacts to things that are surprising and might matter, and helps pull you off whatever you were doing.
regions.why: This is the circuitry a notification is designed to hit. Surprise does not wait politely for you to finish — it can interrupt, and you do not get a vote.
regions.caveat: This patch turns up in several very different areas of research. We only use its interrupting role here.

regions.name: Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex
regions.summary: Holds on to what you are trying to do.
regions.role: Behind your forehead. It keeps the current goal alive while everything else competes for your attention, and tilts the rest of the brain in favour of whatever matters right now.
regions.why: The feeling of concentrating is mostly this: something holding a goal steady against interference. It is hard work, and it does not last long on its own.
regions.caveat: Nothing is stored here. Holding something in mind looks like an active, fragile process spread across the brain, not a note in a drawer.

regions.name: Anterior Cingulate Cortex
regions.summary: Notices when things clash, go wrong, or start costing effort.
regions.role: Buried in the middle, between the two halves. It reacts when two responses are fighting, when you make a mistake, and when things turn out worse than you expected — and it is linked to trying harder afterwards.
regions.why: That moment of slowing down when a task suddenly gets confusing is this kind of signal. Something noticed the clash and spent a little more effort.
regions.caveat: There are several competing accounts of what this signal is actually computing. We show one well-supported version of the story.

regions.name: Ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex
regions.summary: Works out what something is worth here, and calms things down.
regions.role: Low down at the front. It helps judge how good or bad an option is *given the situation*, and it is part of the circuitry that settles a fear response back down afterwards.
regions.why: Being frightened is not just a switch being flipped. Something also has to turn it back off, and that is a job too.
regions.caveat: This is not 'the rational part overriding the emotional part'. The influence runs both ways and depends heavily on the situation.

regions.name: Orbitofrontal Cortex
regions.summary: Asks whether something is worth it right now.
regions.role: Sits just above your eye sockets. It tracks how good an outcome is likely to be — and it updates that as your state changes. The same meal is worth a lot when hungry and very little when full.
regions.why: Worth is not a property of the thing. It is worked out fresh each time, and the answer can change within minutes.
regions.caveat: This region and the one above it overlap a great deal, both anatomically and in the research. We separate them here for clarity.

regions.name: Insular Cortex
regions.summary: Keeps track of how your body feels from the inside.
regions.role: Folded away under the side of the brain. It collects signals about your heartbeat, breathing, stomach and temperature, and is closely tied to how those states feel.
regions.why: A racing heart is not only a result of being alarmed. It is also an input — part of why the feeling has the particular texture it has.
regions.caveat: We are describing a link between body signals and feeling. We are not claiming this region produces feelings by itself.

regions.name: Amygdala
regions.summary: Works out fast whether something matters. Not a 'fear centre'.
regions.role: A small almond-shaped cluster deep in each side. It judges very quickly whether something is worth reacting to, learns which things tend to lead to which outcomes, and sets off a coordinated response in the body and in attention.
regions.why: It answers fast, on bad information. That is worth it when being slow could kill you — and it is also why a stick on a path can read as a snake for half a second.
regions.caveat: Calling this 'the fear centre' is wrong twice over. It does far more than fear, fear involves far more than it, and people whose amygdala is damaged can still feel afraid.

regions.name: Hippocampus
regions.summary: Ties an experience together so you can find it again later.
regions.role: A curled structure deep in each side. Without it you cannot form new memories of things that happen to you. Its job is tying the pieces — what, where, when — into one thing you can pull back up as a whole.
regions.why: People who lose it can still hold a conversation and still learn new skills. They just stop being able to turn their morning into a memory. That split is how we know memory is not one thing.
regions.caveat: Memories are not kept here and then moved somewhere else later. Nothing is copied. What changes over time is which connections retrieval depends on.

regions.name: Entorhinal Cortex
regions.summary: The doorway in and out of the memory system.
regions.role: The main way through between the hippocampus and the rest of the brain. Nearly everything heading into memory goes in this way, and nearly everything coming back out comes out this way.
regions.why: Being a bottleneck has a cost. This is one of the first places affected in some memory disorders, and the effects show up early because so much depends on it.
regions.caveat: Shown as a single gate. It has distinct parts, including cells that fire in a startlingly regular grid as you move through space.

regions.name: Medial Parietal Cortex
regions.summary: Rebuilds the scene when you remember or imagine something.
regions.role: Tucked into the midline near the back. Busy when you recall a detailed memory, picture a place, or think about a situation that is not happening now.
regions.why: Remembering and imagining use much of the same machinery. That is not a coincidence — remembering *is* a kind of building, and this is some of the building.
regions.caveat: What this network is really for is still being worked out. 'Building a scene' is one interpretation among several.

regions.name: Thalamus
regions.summary: The switchboard almost everything passes through.
regions.role: An egg-shaped cluster right in the middle of each side. Nearly all traffic between the deep brain and the surface goes through it, and it adjusts what gets through depending on how awake you are.
regions.why: The difference between being awake, asleep and under anaesthetic lives largely in the loops running through here. The gate is not a side detail — it may be part of what being conscious requires.
regions.caveat: Drawn as one body. It is dozens of clusters with very different jobs, and calling it 'the relay' badly undersells how much it changes what passes through.

regions.name: Hypothalamus
regions.summary: Runs your body's settings — and your body clock.
regions.role: Tiny, sitting right at the base. It controls hormones and the automatic systems that run without you, and it holds the circuitry that decides whether you are awake or asleep.
regions.why: 'Fight or flight' and 'time for bed' are not just turns of phrase. They are switches, in a specific place, that can be found and studied.
regions.caveat: About the size of an almond, and doing an enormous number of unrelated jobs. One node here stands in for many distinct clusters.

regions.name: Basal Ganglia
regions.summary: Picks one action and holds the others back.
regions.role: A set of clusters deep under the surface, wired into loops with the rest of the brain. They help choose between competing actions, release the winner, and learn over time which choices tend to work out.
regions.why: Choosing is as much about suppressing as selecting. When this circuitry goes wrong you get either too little movement or too much — the same failure, in both directions.
regions.caveat: Shown as a single node. The real wiring has several routes through it that partly oppose each other.

regions.name: Cerebellum
regions.summary: Predicts what a movement will feel like, and fixes the difference.
regions.role: The dense, finely ridged lump at the back and bottom. It holds most of the brain's cells. It guesses what a movement should feel like, compares that against what actually happened, and corrects the gap.
regions.why: Feedback from your body arrives too late to steer with. Smooth movement needs a prediction — which is why your hand arrives where you aimed instead of wobbling around it.
regions.caveat: Not only about movement. Its role in language, attention and thinking is an active and surprising area of research.

regions.name: Superior Colliculus
regions.summary: A fast, rough shortcut for turning toward things.
regions.role: A small layered structure in the midbrain. It combines what you see, hear and feel into a rough sense of *where*, and drives quick movements of your eyes and head toward it.
regions.why: It can start you turning before you have worked out what the thing is. Your head moves first; recognising it catches up afterwards.
regions.caveat: The fast shortcut is well supported for orienting. Claims that it can recognise things in any detail are disputed.

regions.name: Brainstem
regions.summary: Keeps you alive, and keeps the rest of the brain switched on.
regions.role: The stalk connecting brain to spinal cord. Everything travelling between your brain and your body passes through it, and it contains the clusters that control breathing, heart rate, and how alert the whole brain is.
regions.why: Every other thing in this simulation depends on the brainstem keeping the system in a state where it can work at all. It is the least glamorous and least optional part.
regions.caveat: One node here stands in for many clusters that differ in both position and chemistry.

regions.name: Noradrenergic Arousal System
regions.summary: Changes the settings of the whole brain at once.
regions.role: A tiny cluster in the brainstem with connections reaching almost everywhere. How active it is tracks how alert and vigilant you are, and whether you are locked on to a task or scanning around.
regions.why: Not every brain signal is a message. Some are settings — and this one changes how everything else responds, everywhere, at the same time.
regions.caveat: Describing it as a volume knob is a convenient picture. The real influence is chemical, slower, and far more uneven than that suggests.

regions.name: Effector / Musculature
regions.summary: Where the signal finally becomes something that moves.
regions.role: Your spinal cord and muscles. Commands coming down get turned into actual force here. The spinal cord also handles some corrections entirely by itself, without asking the brain.
regions.why: Not all of the control is in your head. Some loops are handled locally because going all the way up to the brain and back would simply take too long.
regions.caveat: Not part of the brain at all. It is here because a model of action that stops at the skull is not a model of action.
